Guthrie, O. T., August 1.—(Special) What appears to be a reliable "Zip Wyatt adventure" has come to light. Zip Wyatt and Charley Black, his desperado chum, have at last been found, beyond a doubt. The discovery was made yesterday by two farmers named Nicholson and Parker, eighteen miles west of O'Keene, Blaine county. Nicholson and Black crept up to within a few feet of the outlaws, while they were asleep, and ordered them to throw up their hands. The hands went up promptly, but each pair of them held a Winchester, and in less than no time Nicholson was killed and the bandits were in full flight toward the Glass mountains. Parker claims to have planted about a pint of shot in Black's face and breast, and says that for several miles he left a trail of blood. One hundred men are now in pursuit. Deputy marshals have gone from El Reno to be in at the final round-up, which they think cannot be long delayed. More women still continue to come into the Oklahoma jails. The last are Laura Martin and Pearl Keeper. Deputy United States Marshal E. S. Morris and posse came over from El Reno yesterday with four United States prisoners. They are: Laura Martin, Pearl Keeper, W. B. Miner and Cheatham Pope. The girls are of the demi-mode type and the boys were along as business managers for them. They were on a little excursion through the Cheyenne country when the marshals arrested them as intruders.
E. A. Williams of Washita county, who has been prospecting all over northwestern Oklahoma for gold during the past three months, writes to the Cloud Chief Herald of his discoveries as follows under recent dates:

"I have juset returned from a trip further out northwest, G. W. Ohampett, H. J. Eastwood, J. E. Reynolds and myself, prospecting and surveying out claims. We made a new discovery in Mills county, we found gold and silver in lumps as large as grains of corn, and on a creek called by the Spaniard "Kaskarado," we found ancient mines which had been worked by the Spaniards before the Mexican war. The old furnaces which were use by them for smelting are plain to the seen yet, and signs of a village of about 1,000 inhabitants were found at this place. We have located rich mines. I learned yesterday that the old Spanish town on Turkey creek had been found. We are getting along as well as can be expected under the circumstances; we still find gold and are not in the least discouraged. Good rains in the west; everything looking well; corn is fine; roasting ears as large as your arm.

E. A. WILLIAMS."

MURDER OF MRS. MITCHELL.

The particulars of the murder of Mrs. Mitchell near Choctaw City are given by the Oklahoma City Times-Journal.

J. F. Mitchell and wife lived about six and a half miles northwest of Choctaw City on a fine farm in the black jacks. They were prosperous and surrounded by relatives and neighbors, by whom they were highly respected Therl only daughter, Mrs. Frank Beebe, lives on a claim adjoining on the north, a sister of the murdered woman on the east, and other relatives a short distance away.

Mr. Mitcheel has two houses on this claim, one pretty well toward the eastern edge of his claim, in which lived a colored family by the name of Adkins, who was farming some of the land and had contracted to clear off 30 or 40 acres more. The house in which he himself was living was on the southwest corner of the place. The home of Mr. VanWinters, on the east, the house being well toward the northwest corner, while on the claim to the north, a few rods away from VanWinters house is the house of J. W. Wheeler.

There is a road that goes by these two houses down toward the south edge of the Mitchell claim, and through Mr. Mitchell's pasture to his house.

In the southwest corner of the VanWinters claim, a few rods away from the road "We" Adkins was at work grubbing. Mrs. Beebe had been at Mrs. Mitchell's in the afternoon, and Mrs. Mitchell's went home with her, going by way of Wheeler's to get one of the girls to go over to stay with her daughter, Mrs. Beebe. About 4 o'clock Mrs. Mitchell left Wheeler's to return home, coming back by way of VanWinters, leaving back the latter place shortly after 5 o'clock, by herself to go home through the pasture road.

With the remark, "My wife is murdered," from Mr. Mitchell, the two started down the road on the search and found her about half way through the field, face downward, some peaches she had been carrying, by her side, her bonnet partly on her head, while there was evidence of a heavy blow on the back of the neck from a club, it having cut a small hole through the bonnet. A small pool of blood showed that she had not moved after the stroke. Her right cheek was bruised, and there was a gash on her chin. The body was permitted to lay as found until the storm came up at 2 o'clock, when it was carried to the house.

name of Jones going to the Adkins house and telling him of the murder. The old man was astonished but the two boys received the news with indifference. Mr. Jones told them that the blood hounds would be brought and the right parties found which seemed to have its effect, for soon after "We" Adkins got his shoes and started off towards Choctaw City, going through the corn field. As suspicion rested upon him, persons were sent out to watch him, and he was finally captured a mile or so from home by one of the neighbors. He was immediately taken before a justice to give him a preliminary hearing, but Deputy Sheriff Cannon and Deputy Marshals Hopkins and Gault arrived and demanded the prisoner, but Constable Dobbs claimed him. After considerable talk the preliminary was put off and the prisoner taken to Choctaw City to await examination this afternoon. Two brothers of this boy were afterwards arrested and were held with the one already captured.

The people are greatly wrought up, and demands were made that the prisoner be turned over to them. Last even one could see squads of horsemen here and there going toward Choctaw City. All that was necessary to have caused them to take the law in their own hands would have been absolute certainty that they had the right man.

These circumstances point strongly to "We" Adkins as the murderer. He had had a difficulty with Mr. Mitchell a few weeks before in which Mr. Mitchell had knocked him down. They had threatened to get even, and it is said that he tried to buy a revolver. He was working in a field near weher Mrs. Mitchell passed. A woman, and a man wearing a shirt similar to the one he wore were seen coming down the road. Adkins appeared at VanWinters house at 6 o'clock to get a drink of water and went home from there, something he had never done before. He attempted to escape in the morning before he was accused of the deed, and the fact that the poor woman was not disturbed after being hit, showing the object must have been revenge, all make out a strong case against him that will require strong evidence to clear away. The report that the woman was ravished is not verified by the evidence. She had some peaches with her that lay at her side when she was found which she would have dropped had there been a previous struggle. Her clothing was not disarranged, nor was there any evidence of a struggle. Everything goes to show that the villain came up behind her, struck her with the club, and left her as she fell.

A TERRIBLE CRIME.
Mrs. J. F. Mitchell Assaulted and Murdered Near Oklahoma City.

OKLAHOMA CITY, Ok., July 31.—One of the most fiendish and dastardly crimes ever committed in Oklahoma Territory was perpetrated last night sixteen miles west of this city. Mrs. J. F. Mitchell, a most estimable lady, 42 years of age, was assaulted and murdered. Her husband works at Choctaw City, five miles distant from the claim upon which they live, and when he arrived home he found his wife absent. After inquiring and finding no trace of her, he organized a searching party. Her body was found in a clump of bushes in a pasture lying face downward in the sand. An ugly wound on the back of her head and discolored marks on her throat showed how she had met her death. The ground was torn up considerably, showing that she had made a desperate fight for her life and her honor. "We" Atkins, a colored man who lived on the claim and worked for Mitchell, was arrested, charged with the crime, which he denied, but circumstantial evidence points very strongly to his guilt.
atkins-brothers-oklahoma-city-1895-08-01.A7: The funeral of Mrs. Mitchell, who was murdered near Choctaw City, was held Wednesday and was largely attended. The preliminary examination of the Atkins boys, charged with the murder, will be held Aug. 20.
atkins-brothers-oklahoma-city-1895-08-01.A8: "We" Atkins, charged with the murder of Mrs. Mitchell, at Choctaw City, has been removed from the jail at Oklahoma City to El Reno for safe keeping.

The republicans of Utah in convention at Salt Lake City nominated Heber M. Wells, of that city, for governor. The resolutions demand the free and unlimited coinage of silver.

Robert A. Burch, managing editor of the Brooklyn (N. Y.) Eagle, died at the age of 44 years.

At Lewisburg, Tenn., Jerry Johnson (colored) was lynched by a mob for making an insulting proposal to a white girl.

Mrs. Mercy Prindle died at the home of her son near Castleville, Ia., aged 105 years.

The feature of the second day of the Knights Templar encampment in Boston was the competitive drill. The grand treasurer's report showed cash resources of $30,302.

A boat upset in a squall on the St. Clair river near Marysville, Mich., and Mrs. Michael Derufg, Frank Derufg, her brother-in-law, and Miss Celia Choniski and Miss Edith Connors were drowned.

The funeral of Dr. Simon Quinlain, founder of the Benevolent Order of Elks, took place at East Palmyra, N. Y.

William Haygood, while profaning at High Shoals, Ga., declaring there was no God, no Heaven and no hell, had his tongue paralyzed.

A tornado at Syracuse N. Y., destroyed a large amount of property and caused the loss of several lives.
At Itasca, Tex., John Brown, 23 years old, cut the throat of Miss Boone, aged 13, and then killed himself. Refusal of the girl's father to a marriage was the cause.

A futile attempt was made to wreck an east-bound night express on the Nickle-Plate road near McComb, O.

Willard, George B. Orlady, John J. Wickham and Howard J. Reeder for superior court judges. LYNCHED IN COLQUITT COUNTY.
A Confession of Crime Followed by Enforcement of Mob Law.
A Confession of Crime Followed by Enforcement of Mob Law.

Moultrie, Ga., Aug. 13.—For the first time in its history our county was disturbed and its fair named soiled by a lynching last Saturday, Aug. 10. It is hard to get particulars of the affair, which occurred in the western edge of the county, about eleven miles from here, but from what we can gather, the facts are about these: A negro named John Harris committed an assault on an elderly white lady in the western part of the county, on Friday last, and escaped into Mitchell county, but was pursued and captured by a bailiff from this county. The bailiff was proceeding to the jail here with his prisoner when, in passing the vicinity of his crime (Saturday morning), a number of unknown men took his prisoner from him and proceeded down the road. In about half an hour the bailiff heard several shots fired in the direction taken by the party, and, upon going some distance down the road, he found the body of his late prisoner riddled with shot. He came to Mountricle, reported the facts, and asked for a jury of inquest. The coroner summoned a jury, made an investigation, and returned a verdict substantially as given above. The negro confessed his crime, was identified by his victim, and the lynching is taken as a natural and inevitable consequence of the crime committed.
john-harris-camilla-1895-08-10.A22:
LYNCHED.
A Brutal Negro Perishes at the Hands of a Georgia Mob.
A Brutal Negro Perishes at the Hands of a Georgia Mob.

SAVANNAH, Ga., Aug. 14.—A special from Albany, Ga., says: A horrible crime has been perpetrated near Hurbfield Mill. Last Friday afternoon John Harris, 18 years old, a negro boy, went to the house of Mrs. John Monroe, a highly respected white woman aged 65 years, and after choking her to insensibility outraged her. Mrs. Monroe died a few hours afterward, but before dying regained consciousness long enough to tell who her assailant was. While Harris was committing the crime the screams of his victim were heard by neighbors who arrived in time to see the fiend leave the premises. Being well known his identification was complete, and the alarm soon spread. A posse of 200 men was soon in pursuit. He was captured near Camilla Saturday and taken back to Colquitt county, and on the route he was disposed of. Reports are conflicting as to the method employed, one being that he was burned to death and another that he was cut and shot into giblets and then hung. Whether either of these reports are true or not, it is true that the brute met his death with short shrift after he was captured. His victim was a highly respected woman and her age and infirmities should have protected her against even the desires of a brute.

morris-slater-alias-railroad-bill-identi.A1:
IS RAILROAD BILL DEFUNCT?
A NEGRO KILLED WHO IS THOUGHT TO BE THE DESPERADO.
A Young Sheriff's Officer Mortally Wounds Him After Receiving a Terrible Wound at the Negro's Hands—"Are You Railroad Bill?" I May Be, and I May Not Be," Replied the Dying Man, Who Answers Bill's Description Fairly Well.

Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 16.—To-night the body of a negro who possibly may be Morris Slater, alias "Railroad Bill," the notorious desperado, murderer and train robber of South Alabama, arrived here from Chipley, Ga.

Yesterday the negro was killed near that place by young Willis Garner, one of the sheriff's posse, who came upon him in a deserted house. The darkey opened fire upon Garner with a pistol, shooting him in the abdomen and, after falling to the ground dangerously wounded, the young man returned the fire, one of the bullets penetrating the negro's cnest and coming out at the back of his neck. "Railroad Bill," if it is he, lived about six hours, and when asked by the sheriff: "Are you Railroad Bill?" he replied: "I may be, and I may not." This is all the satisfaction that could be obtained from the dying man.

It is said that the clothes he wore answered the description of Bill's latest reported attire, while in his pockets were several circulars announcing the reward of $1,250 which is set upon the head of the desperado. Six dollars and a ticket to Pensacola, Fla., were also found among his effects. The body was looked at by the road's employes, and they are in doubt as to the dead darkey being Railroad Bill, though the hight, color and size of the man and a scar under his left eye tally with Railroad Bill's description. Mortification has set in and the features of the corpse are puffed out of shape.
morris-slater-alias-railroad-bill-identi.A2:
RAILROAD BILL'S' BODY

Is What the Crowd Went to the Depot to See.

THE COFFIN LID TAKEN OFF

And a Large Yellow Negro Exposed—It Was Not the Corpse of the Redoubta-ble Desperado.
Montgomery, Aug. 16.—(Special.)—Much excitement was caused here tonight by the announcement that "Railroad Bill's" dead body would reach here on the Western train tonight. As the train rolled up an unpainted pine coffin was taken off and the crowd pushed up to see the dead desperado.

Billie West, Mr. Rowle and other railroad men who know "Railroad Bill" were on hand to identify him. When the coffin lid was removed the body of a large yellow negro answering Bill's description in many particulars, although much lighter in complexion, was revealed. The identifiers promptly agreed that the body was not that of the much desired Bill.

The negro was killed on Thursday near Chipley, Ga. A deputy constable there and a young man acquaintance had learned that a negro answering "Railroad Bill's" description had been for a day or two occupying an abandoned hut near there. They determined to get him and accordingly went there Thursday afternoon. As they approached the hut they called to the negro to surrender. He replied by firing a ball into the young man's stomach. The latter fell to the ground, but immediately arose and, taking deliberate aim, fired a Winchester ball through the negro's breast, inflicting a wound from which he died in a few hours. Before he died he was asked if he was "Railroad Bill."

"Maybe I am and maybe not," was the only reply he would give.

It is believed the negro is Thomas, the man who killed the Florida sheriff recently. The names of the constable and his assistant are not stated.
morris-slater-alias-railroad-bill-identi.A5:
The Identity of That Negro.
A negro named E. Culpepper of Chipley, Ga., has written to Mrs. William Thomas, colored, of Mobile informing her that the man who was killed at Chipley last week under suspicion of being "Railroad Bill" was her husband; that he so confessed on his deathbed to Culpepper and asked him to inform his (Thomas') wife of the facts leading up to his death. Culpepper's letter concludes: "The colored people here desire to know if there was anything like a crime against him. Please answer at once, so that we can understand the matter."

Thomas, it seems, worked in Mobile in the capacity of a vessel loader. During the latter part of July a warrant was issued charging him with disorderly conduct and about the same time he lost his job and went to Georgia to hunt work, so his wife says. His wife says he did not know "Railroad Bill," but was a hard working, well behaved negro. The information from Mobile is that he has no crime charged against him there.
morris-slater-alias-railroad-bill-identi.A7:
Thought to Be "Railroad Bill."
Marshal Hardy left Chipley, Ga., the other day, for Montgomery, taking with him the body of the negro who was killed by Willis Garner in the four-cornered fight. It is believed that the negro is "Railroad Bill," who had been such a terror to everybody in southern Alabama during the past two or three years. He had in his pockets a proclamation offering rewards for "Railroad Bill" amounting to $1,250.

sol-russell-1895-08.A1:
GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
NEWS OF THE TWO STATES TOLD IN PARAGRAPHS.
GEORGIA.

An artesian well will soon afford pure water for Statesboro.

The steeple on the Methodist church on West Main street, Statesboro, was struck by lightning on Aug. 8.

Columbus will hold an election on Dec. 14 for the proposition to issue bonds to the amount of $300,000 with which to build new water works.

Georgia Cracker: The board of education half a century ago was a pine shingle. It was found to be a wonderful assistant in teaching the young idea how to shoot.

Covington Star: Jack Belcher of Anderson had three fine hogs killed by lightning one evening last week. Besides those killed, a number of other hogs were badly shocked by the electric bolt.

Worth County Local: Lumber is being placed on the grounds at Poulan for the erection of a mill that will run 180 looms to start with and will increase its machinery as fast as practicable.

Journal: Atlanta wants no strife at this time, especially none on that question which tears a community to pieces worse than any other sort of contest. Let the liquor ordinance stand just as it is.

Gordon County Citizen: A man was discovered kissing his wife on the street in Atlanta the other day and the proceed-
Talbotton News: Talbot is one of the few counties whose digest shows an increase over 1894. This gain of $75,000 is due to the energy of our receiver and the experience of his able assistant, W. S. Brown.

Washington Gazette: Our canning factory started up Wednesday and on the first day put up 625 cans of fruits and vegetables. This is making a remarkably good beginning and the enterprise is bound to be a great success.

Gainesville Cracker: There is an increasing demand for farming lands in this county. This demand is coming from a good class of citizens in this state and the western states, and every advantage should be extended purchasers.

Sparta Ishmaelite: The fellow who approves of bathing costumes for girls on the beach and reprobates bicycle costumes for them on the boulevard is capable of drawing some very nice distinctions. It is a matter of tweedledum and tweedledee.

Covington Star: An unknown young man was found dead two miles below Social Circle by the track of the Georgia railroad on Sunday morning. He is supposed to have fallen off the excursion train Saturday night, and was killed by the fall.

The mayor of Albany is not having a dull time just now. The officials are arresting everybody who has not paid his street tax, and all the cows found at large are being impounded. There are more mad men in Albany than you can imagine.

A young colored man entered the post-office at Statesboro a few days ago, and purchased a postal card, then asked the clerk how much it would cost to send it by mail. Also a white gentleman purchased 30 cents worth of stamps, then asked the postmaster would they go by express or mail.

Ringgold New South: If Dr. Hawthorne, the Atlanta divine, is bitterly opposed to women adopting things that are masculine why don't he show that he is opposed to things that are effiminate in mankind by having his long, black curly locks amputated by a barber? His caustic criticisms might then have more weight with the public.

Jonesboro Enterprise: Clayton county will produce the largest corn crop in its history this year, if the present indications hold good. The county is almost one vast field of the hominy-making product. Hogs are fine here, too—one man reports a litter of nineteen pigs. For hog and hominy, Clayton was never in better shape—even if we are under the depression of the single gold standard.

J. H. Devire has filed suit at Atlanta in the circuit court of the United States against J. B. Glover, receiver of the Marietta and North Georgia Railway Company, asking for $10,000 damages for injuries received by him on June 20, 1894. The plaintiff was a locomotive engineer in the employ of the receiver, and he alleges that he was damaged by the explosion of his engine's boiler, which, he says, was defective. Burton Smith represents the plaintiff.

Toccoa News: We think we can now safely announce that the proposed cotton factory for Toccoa is an assured fact. It is proposed to capitalize the company at $100,000, nearly all of which has been taken. Northern cotton mills are paying handsome dividends, in spite of the fact that they have to pay freights on raw material, high salaries to officers and have many other disadvantages to contend with, and it is very certain that mills in the south, if properly managed, will pay nicely.

Augusta Chronicle: Rev. H. L. Embry, pastor of St. Luke's Methodist church in West End, delivered a strong sermon Sunday night against the tendencies of the age which are involving women in bloomers and leading them to adopt the fashions and modes of men. The recent base ball game in West End between the female nine and a West End team was the subject of severe criticism. The wearing of bloomers and the riding of bicycles were denounced in strong and unmistakable language.

Journal: A desperate duel was fought in Atlanta Monday morning at 9:30 o'clock on South Pryor street, the principals being James L. Hight, Jr., and Will Strickland, a negro. Hight was armed with a double barrelled shot gun, while the negro used a repeating Winchester rifle. Four shots were exchanged, two on each side. Hight was unhurt, but the negro was badly injured, being literally peppered with shot. Both men were arrested and taken to the police station. The affair created intense excitement in the neighborhood.

A fine horse belonging to James Parker was badly injured by an electric shock on Broad street in West End, Augusta, Saturday afternoon. The trolley of a Harrisburg car flew off and broke a telephone wire. This latter wire fell across some railway guy wire and one end of it lay on the ground. The motorman continued along and when the horse, driven along with a wagon, touched the wire he was knocked down by the shock. The animal fell several times and was painfully burned. The horse is now under the treatment of a veterinary.

Star: Frank Patrick shot Sol Russell, a desperate negro, in Brick Store district, near Covington, Saturday. Mr. Patrick, with several other men, had surrounded the house in which Sol was located, for the purpose of arresting him, when the negro ran out, with a Winchester rifle. Mr. Patrick being the first man he saw, Sol deliberately raised his gun and fired at him, but before he could shoot again Mr. Patrick returned the fire, hitting the negro in the face and eyes with bird shot. Sol is now in jail in Covington, and is under treatment of Drs. J. A. Wright and W. D. Travis, who think he may probably lose one eye. He is a bad negro, and has not been out of the "gang" but a short while.
